A Christmas murder mystery logic puzzle for one: 2,807 people in a grand hotel on Christmas Eve, 18 clues, and one visitor to the Tower Suite.

The Corliss has stood on Founders Square since 1903, and on Christmas Eve it is the busiest building in the city. Gerald Fernandez started there in 1979 as a front desk clerk in a borrowed suit and finished as chairman of the company that owns it. Every Christmas Eve he gives the toast at the Gala, and every Christmas Eve he sleeps alone in the Tower Suite at the top of the building. His toast always ends the same way: "The Corliss never forgets a face."

Tonight he rides the Tower Lift up to his suite and asks for no one at the door until half past ten. At 10:37 his butler finds him on the sitting room floor. His little silver pill box is nowhere in the room.

Snow has closed the roads, the night manager holds every door, and the front desk prints the Christmas Eve House List: every guest, every Gala ticket, every member of staff and every entertainer. One of those 2,807 people rode the Tower Lift up to Gerald Fernandez, and came back down without him.

You were the Corliss's night concierge for years. You know which key opens which door. Work through the House List, follow 18 clues, and find the one person left standing.

CASE AT A GLANCE
• 2,807 suspects · 18 clues · 1 killer
• Difficulty: Medium-Hard (4 of 5 stars)
• Play time: about 3 to 6 hours, easy to split over a few evenings
• Players: 1 (or work it together as a pair)
• Day 11 of 12 Days of Murder. Every case stands on its own.

WHAT YOU GET
• Case File (85 pages): the story, the evidence timeline, how to play, five reference pages, the House List, the 18 clues, an elimination tracker with checkpoints, hint cards and a Case Closed page
• Solution File (5 pages): the reveal, how every clue proves it, who each clue ruled out, and what really happened
• Both files in US Letter and A4

HOW IT WORKS
1. Print the Case File, or mark it up on a tablet.
2. Read the story, the evidence and the reference pages.
3. Apply each clue's bold rule to the House List and cross out everyone it rules out. Some rules send you to a reference page first.
4. Play the clues in any order. Checkpoints tell you if your count is on track.
5. Name the one person left, then open the Solution File.

Stuck? Eight hint cards nudge you toward how to read a clue without giving away who did it.

WHAT MAKES THIS CASE DIFFERENT
• A whole hotel on Christmas Eve. Guests, visitors, staff and performers all sit on one list, with 13 details each: room, dinner, bar tab, key, turndown and more.
• Real detective work. Hotel keys, bar hours, the Gala seating plan and the Christmas Eve program all matter, and several clues make you look things up before you strike a single name.
• A bigger case for a longer evening. This is a Full Case, built to be picked up and put down, with checkpoints to keep you on track.
• One killer, and the clues are fair: every one is needed, and the answer is the same in whatever order you play them.

PERFECT FOR
• Logic puzzle and whodunit fans who want a longer, meatier case
• Solo evenings with a pen and a cup of cocoa
• Christmas gifts for the puzzler who has everything
• Anyone collecting the full 12 Days of Murder

GOOD TO KNOW
